title: Bank-conflict and warp-imbalance probe: attention kernel sensitivity
body:
Context:
Quick exploratory probe into micro-architectural sources of tail latency and throughput drops in attention kernels. Prior work flagged cases where FlashAttention and paged-attention fused paths exhibit higher p95 for medium sequence lengths (128–512) and certain batch/seq length mixes. This doc captures a set of small, focused experiments aimed at detecting shared-memory bank conflicts, warp imbalance, and per-block divergence as contributing factors.

Goals and hypothesis:
- Hypothesis 1: For paged attention with dynamic page boundaries, misaligned reads/writes into shared memory produce repeated bank conflicts that degrade throughput for specific sequence mod patterns (e.g., seq%32 in [1..4]).
- Hypothesis 2: When fused ops (matmul + softmax + scale) run with thread-block sizes chosen for peak gfLOPS, irregular sequence lengths create warp imbalance leading to SM underutilization and latency jitter.
- Hypothesis 3: Padding/alignment tricks that reduce bank conflicts should measurably improve p50/p95 for affected workloads without regressing long-tail for very long sequences.

Environment and hardware:
- Cluster: dev-gpu-cluster-prod-sim (single GPU test nodes)
- GPU: A100-SXM4-80GB, driver 525.xx, CUDA 12.1
- Serving runtime: branch perf/attn-bank-probe (commit 9a7f3d)
- Kernels under test: flash_attn_v2 (fused), paged_attn_prefetch (paged), fused-matmul-softmax (legacy fused)
- Tools: Nsight Systems (nsys), nvprof (for counters), CUPTI sampling via our tracebench harness, `perf` on CPU side to rule out dispatch stalls.

Microbench harness (how to reproduce):
- repo: serving-runtime/perf/attn_microbench
- command examples:
  - python run_microbench.py --model=gpt2 --kernel=flash --batch=8 --seq=128 --warm=200 --iters=1200 --coalesce=false
  - python run_microbench.py --model=gpt2 --kernel=paged --batch=6 --seq=136 --page-size=64 --prefetch=2
- nsys capture: nsys profile -o out.nsys-rep --trace=cuda,osrt --stats=true python run_microbench.py ...
- nvprof counter capture (sample): nvprof --metrics achieved_occupancy,branch_efficiency,sm_efficiency,shared_load_transactions,shared_store_transactions -- python run_microbench.py ...

Experiment matrix (subset):
- Vary sequence lengths [64, 96, 128, 136, 192, 256, 384, 512]
- Vary batch sizes [1,2,4,6,8,12] while keeping tokens per second approx constant for some runs
- Toggle padding alignment: none, pad to 32, pad to 64 (pad on GPU by copying into aligned buffer)
- Toggle shared-memory layout: packed (default) vs interleaved (insert 1-word gap between rows)
- Kernel variants: flash (v2), paged (with prefetch 0/1/2), fused-legacy

Key observations (raw):
- For sequence lengths that are not multiples of 32 (particularly 96, 136), we saw a 12–18% drop in achieved_gflops for the flash kernel compared to neighboring lengths. p95 latency increased ~20–35ms depending on batch.
- nvprof counters showed elevated shared_load_transactions and shared_store_transactions per warp on those lengths, indicating repeated accesses to the same banks across threads. Branch efficiency remained high (~98%), suggesting divergence isn't the immediate culprit.
- Nsight timeline showed that some threadblocks completed much earlier than others for irregular seq lengths (visible as short, unused lanes in the timeline). This aligns with warp imbalance.
- Interleaved shared-memory layout (1-word gap) reduced shared_load_transactions by ~30% on the problematic seq lengths and recovered 8–12% of the lost throughput on flash. However, it increased shared memory footprint ~6% and slightly reduced occupancy.
- Paged-attention with prefetch=2 reduced DRAM stalls on long sequences but did not eliminate the bank conflict effect on medium irregular lengths. This suggests prefetch helps backend bandwidth but not intra-block bank alignment.

Representative numbers (median of 5 runs):
- Kernel: flash, batch=8
  - seq=128: p50=4.6ms, p95=9.8ms, tokens/s=1.2M, achieved_gflops=4200
  - seq=136: p50=5.2ms, p95=13.1ms, tokens/s=1.05M, achieved_gflops=3600
  - seq=136 + interleaved-shm: p50=4.8ms, p95=10.7ms, tokens/s=1.12M, achieved_gflops=3850

- Kernel: paged, batch=6, page-size=64
  - seq=192: p50=7.1ms, p95=15.0ms, DRAM-stall% increased by 9% vs flash
  - seq=192 + prefetch=2: p50=6.8ms, p95=13.2ms

Investigation notes (why we think bank conflicts):
- Shared_load/store counters spiked only for those sequence lengths; correlated with lower achieved gflops and more mem fence/wait times in nsys timeline.
- Divergence/branch metrics are good, so threads are executing similar instruction paths. The imbalance appears when last warp has fewer active lanes due to tail tokens, causing other warps to run extra bookkeeping and some shared memory patterns become hotspot.
- Code patterns using row-major shared tiles with tile width equal to warp-size (32) are most affected when sequence%32 != 0 because accesses from different threads map into the same bank offsets repeatedly.

Quick mitigations tried:
1) Insert padding per row (1 or 2 words) to change stripe mapping — helped but increased shared memory usage.
2) Change load order: staggered thread-to-element mapping (thread t reads element (t*stride) mod tile_width) — reduced bank conflicts but complicated indexing and added minor compute overhead (~1–2%).
3) Fallback policy: detect problematic seq and batch patterns at runtime and switch to an alternate kernel variant (interleaved layout) — cost: extra code paths + marginal occupancy loss. When enabled, p95 improves for the problematic mix but overall median is flat.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Padding reduces conflicts but consumes shared memory, potentially lowering occupancy and hurting very small-batch cases or very long sequences where shared memory is already highly contended.
- Staggered loads add compute overhead; in microbenchmarks cost is manageable but need to evaluate at scale across many customers.
- Introducing layout variants increases complexity in kernel selection heuristics and testing burden.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can we implement a lightweight heuristic in the runtime to detect risky (batch, seq) combos cheaply (e.g., seq%32 in [1..8] and batch between [4..12]) and switch kernels? What is the decision overhead?
- Evaluate on other GPU generations (H100, V100) to see whether bank size/behavior changes the sweet spot.
- Run longer tails for live traffic-like mixes (mixed seq lengths within a batch) to validate multi-tenant and coalesced-batch behavior.
- Check interaction with kv-cache: does kv-copy/paged-shuffling amplify bank hotspots?

Action items (short-term):
- [Anika] Implement interleaved-shm variant in perf branch and add unit test for seq mod patterns (due 2025-11-09).
- [Liam] Add lightweight runtime pattern detector that logs candidate events to tracing (due 2025-11-12).
- [Marco] Re-run matrix on H100 test node and report delta to A100 baseline (due 2025-11-16).
- [Priya] Evaluate impact on Dedicated autoscaling workloads (small-batch heavy) for occupancy regressions (due 2025-11-20).

Notes to self / miscellaneous: 
- Keep an eye on fused op codegen; some of the register allocation choices in the fused path exacerbate shared memory pressure. Might need to tune launch config per-variant.
- Log snippets and sample nsys timeline exports attached to linked artifacts (see PR #942 for traces).

Conclusion (working):
There is credible signal that bank conflicts and warp imbalance drive a meaningful portion of the p95 regressions for medium, misaligned sequence lengths in our attention kernels. Mitigations (interleaving or padding) recover a majority of the perf but introduce resource trade-offs. Next step is a controlled rollout: add detector, enable interleaved variant behind a runtime flag, run a 2-week A/B on synthetic traffic mixes and report production-like regression matrix.

Appendix (commands & snippets):
- sample nvprof capture: nvprof --metrics achieved_occupancy,shared_load_transactions,shared_store_transactions --profile-from-start off -- python run_microbench.py --kernel=flash --seq=136 --batch=8
- sample staggered load pseudocode:
  for t in 0..T-1:
    idx = (t * STRIDE) % TILE_WIDTH
    out[idx] = sdata[idx]\n  where STRIDE chosen such that thread-to-bank mapping disperses accesses.

If you have other ideas for cheap mitigations (e.g., compiler-level padding, warp-level intrinsics), add them inline and I will try them in the perf branch.
